scenes.visual: Title card, at most 2 seconds: lesson name 'Molecular Motors and Cargo' and film title 'Grip, Swing, Let Go'. Behind it, already faint and drifting, the nerve cell of the next scene, so the hook picture is waiting when the card lifts.

scenes.tts: A protein made in a nerve cell's body may have to reach a synapse a metre away. Left to diffuse, it would take centuries, so how does it get there? The cell hands it to a motor, a protein that walks.
scenes.caption: A protein made in a nerve cell's body may have to reach a synapse a metre away. Left to diffuse, it would take centuries, so how does it get there? The cell hands it to a motor, a protein that walks.
scenes.visual: Wide shot filling the frame: a nerve cell body (round blob, left) with one very long axon running right to a synapse knob at the far right edge; label 'up to 1 m (schematic)' under the axon. On 'protein made', a small yellow cargo dot appears in the cell body and starts a random jiggle (Brownian-walk updater) that barely leaves the cell body for the whole sentence. On 'centuries', a counter beside it ticks up and settles on '≈600 years (GFP; 1 m)'. On 'how does it get there', a large question mark pulses at the synapse end. On 'hands it to a motor', the camera dives into the axon: a two-footed motor cartoon (two orange feet on a stalk) grabs the yellow dot and the dot stops jiggling.
scenes.narration: A protein made in a nerve cell's body may have to reach a synapse a metre away. Left to diffuse, it would take centuries, so how does it get there? The cell hands it to a motor, a protein that walks.

scenes.tts: Its road is a microtubule, and the road has a direction. In an axon, nearly every microtubule points its plus end out. Kinesin one walks toward the plus end. Dynein walks toward the minus end, back home.
scenes.caption: Its road is a microtubule, and the road has a direction. In an axon, nearly every microtubule points its plus end out. Kinesin-1 walks toward the plus end. Dynein walks toward the minus end, back home.
scenes.visual: The film's one world: a thick blue microtubule bar spanning the full frame width at mid-height, built from identical tiles that all face the same way (each tile a small chevron pointing right); a faint shimmer runs along it continuously. On 'has a direction', the chevrons light in a wave from left to right. On 'plus end out', a large '+' appears at the right end with 'synapse →' and a '−' at the left end with '← cell body'. On 'Kinesin one walks', the orange two-footed motor (label 'kinesin-1') carrying the yellow cargo starts stepping steadily rightward. On 'Dynein walks', an abstract purple motor icon (label 'dynein') carrying a second cargo dot steps leftward on the same bar; both keep moving to the end of the scene.
scenes.narration: Its road is a microtubule, and the road has a direction. In an axon, nearly every microtubule points its plus end out. Kinesin-1 walks toward the plus end. Dynein walks toward the minus end, back home.

scenes.tts: Watch one foot. It grips the track. It swings while gripping, which pulls the motor forward. Then it lets go and re-cocks. Each turn of this cycle is driven by one A T P.
scenes.caption: Watch one foot. It grips the track. It swings while gripping, which pulls the motor forward. Then it lets go and re-cocks. Each turn of this cycle is driven by one ATP.
scenes.visual: Dynein fades out; zoom in on kinesin until one orange foot and a stretch of blue track fill most of the frame height. A circular four-station dial (GRIP, SWING, LET GO, RE-COCK, size 30+) sits upper right with a pointer. On 'grips the track', the foot settles onto one tile and GRIP lights. On 'swings while gripping', the foot's neck tilts forward on a hinge and the stalk and cargo slide one notch right; SWING lights. On 'lets go', the foot lifts off; LET GO lights. On 're-cocks', the neck rotates back to its starting tilt; RE-COCK lights. On 'one A T P', a green '1 ATP per cycle' badge appears beside the completed dial, without tying ATP binding or hydrolysis to one station; the pointer keeps circling slowly through the stations until the scene ends.
scenes.narration: Watch one foot. It grips the track. It swings while gripping, which pulls the motor forward. Then it lets go and re-cocks. Each turn of this cycle is driven by one ATP.

scenes.tts: So a motor has feet on a polar track, each repeating grip, swing, let go, re-cock. Which way the swing points helps set which way a motor goes, though dynein is less tidy.
scenes.caption: So a motor has feet on a polar track, each repeating grip, swing, let go, re-cock. Which way the swing points helps set which way a motor goes, though dynein is less tidy.
scenes.visual: Zoom back out so the track again spans the frame; the dial shrinks to a corner icon and keeps turning. On 'has feet', both kinesin feet glow. On 'polar track', the chevron wave runs again along the blue bar. On 'Which way the swing points', a curved arrow shows kinesin's swing pointing right (toward '+') and kinesin steps right; the abstract purple dynein icon slides back in on the left and steps left without a simple swing arrow. Both keep stepping to the end.
scenes.narration: So a motor has feet on a polar track, each repeating grip, swing, let go, re-cock. Which way the swing points helps set which way a motor goes, though dynein is less tidy.

scenes.tts: Kinesin one has two feet. The back foot lets go. The front foot, still gripping, swings and tips it past, onto the next site. Then the feet swap roles. Think of walking: your hips move one step, your back foot twice as far.
scenes.caption: Kinesin-1 has two feet. The back foot lets go. The front foot, still gripping, swings and tips it past, onto the next site. Then the feet swap roles. Think of walking: your hips move one step, your back foot twice as far.
scenes.visual: Dynein leaves; close side view of kinesin on the blue track, filling 60%+ of frame height, with tick marks under the track at every binding site (labelled once '8 nm apart'). Back foot light orange, front foot dark orange. On 'back foot lets go', the back foot lifts. On 'still gripping, swings', the front foot's neck tilts forward and the lifted foot arcs over it, landing two ticks from where it started and one tick ahead of the other foot. On 'swap roles', the foot colours swap, and the step then repeats at a slow, steady rhythm. On 'Think of walking', a stick-figure walker fades in above the track, walking in step with the motor: a dot on its hips moves one stride while its back foot swings from behind to in front.
scenes.narration: Kinesin-1 has two feet. The back foot lets go. The front foot, still gripping, swings and tips it past, onto the next site. Then the feet swap roles. Think of walking: your hips move one step, your back foot twice as far.

scenes.tts: The cargo rides at the hips, moving eight nanometres per step. Each foot moves about sixteen. And at low load, each step costs one A T P.
scenes.caption: The cargo rides at the hips, moving 8 nanometres per step. Each foot moves about 16. And at low load, each step costs one ATP.
scenes.visual: Kinesin keeps stepping at a slow, steady rhythm for the whole scene. On 'cargo rides at the hips', a yellow bracket travels with the cargo and reads '8 nm per step'. On 'Each foot moves', an orange bracket follows one foot through a step and reads '≈16 nm'. On 'one A T P', a green ATP chip is spent at each landing and a counter 'steps: n  ATP: n' runs in lockstep, labelled 'low load, in vitro'.
scenes.narration: The cargo rides at the hips, moving 8 nanometres per step. Each foot moves about 16. And at low load, each step costs one ATP.

scenes.tts: Here is the trick. The gripping foot nearly always stays on until the stepping foot lands. So one kinesin can take about a hundred steps before it lets go. A motor that keeps walking like this is called processive.
scenes.caption: Here is the trick. The gripping foot nearly always stays on until the stepping foot lands. So one kinesin can take about 100 steps before it lets go. A motor that keeps walking like this is called processive.
scenes.visual: Inset clears; kinesin keeps stepping. On 'nearly always stays on', the gripping foot glows until the stepping foot lands, when the glow transfers; a small label reads 'nearly always one foot bound'. On 'about a hundred steps', the camera pulls back as the motor walks; a step counter runs from 0 to about 100 and a bracket under the path reads 'under 1 micrometre'; at the end the motor lifts off (label 'about 100 steps, in vitro'). On 'processive', the word appears in large orange type over the path.
scenes.narration: Here is the trick. The gripping foot nearly always stays on until the stepping foot lands. So one kinesin can take about 100 steps before it lets go. A motor that keeps walking like this is called processive.

scenes.tts: Now a test. Muscle myosin two also has two feet. Could one molecule of it carry a vesicle all on its own? Pause and predict.
scenes.caption: Now a test. Muscle myosin II also has two feet. Could one molecule of it carry a vesicle all on its own? Pause and predict.
scenes.visual: The blue microtubule recolours and thins into a green actin filament in the same place (label 'actin'). A red two-footed motor labelled 'myosin II' drops onto it carrying a yellow vesicle. On 'Could one molecule', a question card fades in at the top: 'One myosin II, one vesicle: can it walk?' The motor's feet twitch slowly in place (ambient updater) for the rest of the scene.
scenes.narration: Now a test. Muscle myosin II also has two feet. Could one molecule of it carry a vesicle all on its own? Pause and predict.

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. The question card stays on screen; the red myosin II on the green actin bar idles with a slow breathing motion of its feet; nothing new appears.

scenes.tts: No. Each myosin two foot spends most of its cycle off the track. The two feet do not take turns. One molecule soon falls away. So myosin two works in crowds, hundreds of heads per thick filament.
scenes.caption: No. Each myosin II foot spends most of its cycle off the track. The two feet do not take turns. One molecule soon falls away. So myosin II works in crowds, hundreds of heads per thick filament.
scenes.visual: The question card's 'can it walk?' is crossed out. On 'off the track', each red foot spends most of a loop lifted, touching the actin only briefly and independently of the other; on 'falls away', both are up at once and the motor and vesicle drift off the bottom of the frame. On 'works in crowds', a long gold bar (label 'thick filament') slides in under the actin with many red heads along it (draw about 20, label 'hundreds of heads'); the heads flicker on and off actin out of sync, so at every moment a few are gripping (each touching head glows).
scenes.narration: No. Each myosin II foot spends most of its cycle off the track. The two feet do not take turns. One molecule soon falls away. So myosin II works in crowds, hundreds of heads per thick filament.

scenes.tts: That crowd shortens muscle. Heads grip the thin actin filaments, swing, and let go. The thin filaments slide inward between the thick ones. No filament gets shorter. They just overlap more.
scenes.caption: That crowd shortens muscle. Heads grip the thin actin filaments, swing, and let go. The thin filaments slide inward between the thick ones. No filament gets shorter. They just overlap more.
scenes.visual: The frame widens into one sarcomere (schematic): a white Z line at each side (label 'Z'), green thin filaments anchored to each Z line pointing inward, a gold thick filament in the middle with red heads on both halves. The small GRIP/SWING/LET GO/RE-COCK dial returns in a corner and turns. On 'grip the thin actin', heads flicker on and off as before. On 'slide inward', the green filaments and Z lines move steadily toward the centre for the rest of the scene. On 'No filament gets shorter', a length bracket rides on one green filament and one on the gold filament, each length constant, while the shaded overlap zone widens.
scenes.narration: That crowd shortens muscle. Heads grip the thin actin filaments, swing, and let go. The thin filaments slide inward between the thick ones. No filament gets shorter. They just overlap more.

scenes.tts: Back to the metre. Cargo often carries several motors, so while one lets go, another still holds. How much this matters in cells is still being worked out.
scenes.caption: Back to the metre. Cargo often carries several motors, so while one lets go, another still holds. How much this matters in cells is still being worked out.
scenes.visual: Back to the blue microtubule world of scene 2, track spanning the frame, '+' at right. The yellow cargo now carries three orange kinesins and travels right the whole scene. On 'while one lets go', one kinesin lifts off while the other two keep stepping, then it drops back on. On 'still being worked out', a label 'in cells: open question' appears above the cargo while it keeps moving.
scenes.narration: Back to the metre. Cargo often carries several motors, so while one lets go, another still holds. How much this matters in cells is still being worked out.

scenes.tts: So a motor walks by repeating one small cycle. Keep a foot on the track, and one molecule can travel far. Let go too often, and only a crowd can pull.
scenes.caption: So a motor walks by repeating one small cycle. Keep a foot on the track, and one molecule can travel far. Let go too often, and only a crowd can pull.
scenes.visual: Frame split top and bottom, both moving the whole time. Top: a single orange kinesin walks rightward on the blue microtubule, one foot always glowing on the track (label 'one foot down: walks alone'). Bottom: the red myosin II crowd on the gold thick filament pulls the green actin past (label 'feet mostly off: a crowd'). The four-station dial turns between them. Top half brightens on 'Keep a foot', bottom half on 'Let go too often'.
scenes.narration: So a motor walks by repeating one small cycle. Keep a foot on the track, and one molecule can travel far. Let go too often, and only a crowd can pull.

scenes.visual: End card line: 'Grip, swing, let go, re-cock: keep one foot down to walk alone.' Behind it, faint, the single kinesin keeps stepping along the microtubule.
